title: Measuring the Motor: Finding Gain and Time Constant From a Step, and Knowing How Far to Trust Them

questions.question: Why not use the time constant on the motor's datasheet?
options: It is given for the motor's voltage and not for its command
It is for a motor in the maker's conditions, not yours warmed up and loaded, and a controller tuned on a wrong time constant overshoots on the real one
Datasheets quote the electrical time constant, which is always zero
It changes every time the motor is switched on
questions.explanation: The datasheet's figure is for a bare motor under the maker's conditions. The one that matters is the motor in this machine, with its load.

questions.question: What is the gain, read from a step?
options: The highest speed reached during the step
The slope of the speed in the first few readings
The time the speed takes to reach its final value
The speed it settled to over the command, taking the mean of the last tenth of the readings so one noisy sample does not decide it
questions.explanation: The gain is how much speed a unit of command buys in the end. Averaging the last tenth of the trace gave 1.9991 for a true 2.0.

questions.question: The clean fit gave a time constant of 0.0989 for a motor built with 0.1. Whose error is that?
options: The simulated motor's: Euler at 2 ms makes the effective time constant about half a step shorter, and a measurement of a simulation measures the simulation
The fit's: least squares always reads a little short
The noise's, though the trace was clean
The clock's: the readings were stamped 1 percent late
questions.explanation: Stepped with Euler at 2 ms, a first order system behaves as if its time constant were about half a step shorter. The fit read what was there.

questions.question: At a noise of 0.5 the quick log fit gave 0.222 with a small spread. What does that mean?
options: It is right: a small spread means a good estimate
It is confidently wrong: the logarithm of a noisy number does not average to the logarithm of the number, so the line leans, and the refined fit gave 0.0989
The noise was too large for any method
The trace was too short, and the refined fit gave the same 0.222
questions.explanation: Noise pushes every logged point the same way, so the line is tilted and the answer is biased, not scattered. Searching for the time constant directly gave 0.0989 at every noise level.

questions.question: A model fitted on a step of 1 predicts steps up to a command of 12 to within 0.01 and a command of 20 to within 14.4. Why?
options: The fit was poor to begin with, and the error grows with the command
The time constant gets longer at high commands
The motor clamps its command at 12 and the model has no limit: it is good where it was fitted and the limit is not found by the fit
Noise is proportional to the command
questions.explanation: The model is linear, and the motor is linear only up to its limit of 12. At 20 the motor goes to 24 and the model says 40.

questions.question: Which traces should a fit refuse?
options: Only traces with noise above 0.5
Only traces shorter than one time constant
None: any trace gives some estimate
Too few readings, different lengths, a zero command, a motor that never moved, and a speed already final from the first reading
questions.explanation: Each of those gives no information about the gain or the time constant. A fit that returned numbers for them would be making them up.
